income.magnitude_note: Tax cuts of roughly $4.5 trillion over ten years (JCT); Medicaid and SNAP reductions of more than $1 trillion; CBO net deficit effect about $3.4 trillion. Check the figures against the CBO letter and JCT tables before publishing.
income.justification: CBO's August 2025 distributional analysis found the lowest-income tenth of households loses about $1,600 a year (roughly 4 percent of income), mostly from Medicaid and food-stamp changes, while the highest tenth gains about $12,000 (roughly 2 percent). A bottom group that loses while the top gains sits in the +80 to +100 band. The low end of the range (+35) is the tax title on its own, where JCT shows cuts for every income group with the largest percentage gains in the upper-middle.

sources.ref: Distributional effects of P.L. 119-21, letter of August 2025
Distribution of the tax provisions of H.R. 1, 2025

households_business.magnitude_note: Households: standard deduction, child credit of $2,200, tips/overtime/senior deductions; about 10 million more people uninsured by 2034 (CBO). Business: permanent 100 percent bonus depreciation, immediate write-off of domestic research costs (section 174A), the looser interest-deduction limit (section 163(j) back to an EBITDA base), permanent 20 percent pass-through deduction.
households_business.justification: Most households get a modest tax cut, which is the +30 end of the range. Households that rely on Medicaid or food stamps face new work-reporting rules and state cost shifts that CBO expects to remove coverage from millions, the -60 end. Businesses of every size gain: large corporations from permanent full expensing, research expensing and the interest-deduction change, pass-throughs from the permanent 20 percent deduction. Corporate provisions are counted 25 percent to workers and 75 percent to owners per the rubric.

sources.ref: Cost estimate and coverage effects of P.L. 119-21
Title VII (tax), Title IV (health), Title I (agriculture/SNAP)

plain_json.effective: Tax changes apply to tax year 2025; benefit changes start in 2027

phase_changes.what: SALT deduction cap rises to $40,000 and grows 1 percent a year
Medicaid work-reporting rules start (states may get delays to 2028)
States begin paying a share of food-stamp benefits, scaled to their error rates
Deductions for tips, overtime, seniors and car-loan interest expire

plain_json.sunset: Mixed: individual rate cuts and business provisions are permanent; tips, overtime, senior and car-loan deductions end after 2028; the higher SALT cap ends after 2029
plain_json.delayed_cost: yes - the tax cuts start in 2025 while the largest benefit cuts arrive in 2027 and 2028
plain_json.plain: Most people see the tax cut on their 2025 return; the Medicaid and food-stamp changes do not bite until 2027 and 2028, and several of the new deductions disappear after 2028.

timing.justification: Effective dates from the enacted text: section 70101 onward for tax, sections 71119 (Medicaid community engagement) and 10105 (SNAP state cost share).

flags.plain: Adds an 80-hour-a-month work or activity requirement for many adults on Medicaid, and extends food-stamp work rules to people up to 64 and to parents of children 14 and older.
Makes states pay part of food-stamp benefits from late 2027 and a larger share of administrative costs.
Leaves the details of the Medicaid verification process, the tip and overtime deductions and many credits to Treasury and HHS rules.
Adds about $170 billion for immigration enforcement, including detention capacity and Border Patrol hiring.

rights.justification: Flags taken from the enacted text; the earlier House provision limiting court contempt enforcement was removed in the Senate.

plain_json.one_sentence: Makes the 2017 tax cuts permanent and adds new deductions for tips, overtime and seniors through 2028. Pays for part of it by cutting Medicaid and food stamps starting in 2027.

if_you_are.worker: Your tax rates stay where they are, and if you earn tips or overtime you can deduct part of that pay through 2028.
if_you_are.parent: The child tax credit rises to $2,200 per child and now grows with inflation; food-stamp work rules apply once your youngest child turns 14.
if_you_are.retiree: People 65 and older get an extra $6,000 deduction through 2028; it shrinks above $75,000 of income ($150,000 for couples).
if_you_are.small_business_owner: The 20 percent deduction on business income is now permanent, and equipment and U.S. research costs can be written off in the year you spend them.
if_you_are.disability: Medicaid's new work rules exempt people with disabilities, but proving the exemption is now on you; missing a paperwork check can end coverage.

plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: It did not extend the larger Affordable Care Act premium subsidies, which expired at the end of 2025.

income.justification: The act changes detention rules and who may sue; it has no tax, benefit or wage provisions, so there is no income distribution to score.

households_business.magnitude_note: No CBO estimate of detention costs is on file; an ICE estimate cited during Senate debate put first-year detention costs near $27 billion. Verify before publishing.
households_business.justification: Households with a member who lacks legal status face mandatory detention after an arrest, before any conviction, for theft, shoplifting, assault on an officer, or crimes causing death or serious injury. Most households see no direct effect, which is the 0 end of the range. The act has no provisions aimed at businesses.

plain_json.plain: Applies right away to anyone arrested after the act took effect.

timing.justification: The text sets no start date or expiration.

flags.plain: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to detain non-citizens without legal status who are charged with or arrested for theft, shoplifting, assault on a police officer, or a crime causing death or serious injury, even before a conviction.
Lets a state sue the federal government when an immigration decision, such as releasing someone or granting parole, harms the state or its residents by more than $100.

rights.justification: Sections 2 and 3 of the enacted text as described in the CRS summary.

plain_json.one_sentence: Requires jail for non-citizens who are in the country illegally and get arrested for theft or assault. It also lets states sue the federal government over how it enforces immigration law.

if_you_are.worker: No direct effect unless you or a family member is a non-citizen without legal status.
if_you_are.parent: No direct effect unless a family member is a non-citizen without legal status; an arrest, not a conviction, now triggers detention.

plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: It does not change who can be deported; it changes who must be held in custody while their case proceeds.

income.magnitude_note: JCT put the revenue loss at about $4 billion over ten years (cost estimate on file: CBO publication 61241). Almost all of the lost revenue is tax that would have been collected from crypto gains that now go unreported.
income.justification: The repeal removes IRS reporting of sales on decentralized crypto platforms, so its benefit is lower effective tax on crypto gains. Crypto ownership and especially decentralized-platform use skew toward higher-income and higher-wealth households, and capital-gain relief moves the score positive under the text rules. The effect is small in dollars and reaches a narrow group, which keeps it out of the higher bands.

households_business.magnitude_note: Decentralized-finance platforms avoid building broker reporting systems; users avoid new tax forms; the Treasury loses roughly $4 billion over ten years.
households_business.justification: The main beneficiaries are the platforms, which no longer have to identify users and report their sales, and the traders whose gains stay unreported. Households that use these platforms get less paperwork, a small plus; everyone else bears the revenue loss.

plain_json.sunset: none - the rule is void and a substantially similar rule cannot be issued without a new law
plain_json.plain: The reporting rule, which would have covered sales from 2027 on, never takes effect.

timing.justification: Congressional Review Act disapproval takes effect on enactment and bars a substantially similar rule.

flags.plain: Voids the IRS reporting rule and bars the IRS from issuing a substantially similar one without a new law.

rights.justification: Congressional Review Act disapproval, section 801 of title 5.

plain_json.one_sentence: Cancels an IRS rule that would have made decentralized crypto exchanges report their users' sales to the IRS starting in 2027.

if_you_are.worker: No direct effect unless you trade crypto on decentralized platforms; those platforms will not send you or the IRS a tax form.
if_you_are.small_business_owner: If you run a decentralized crypto service, you no longer have to collect customer identities and report their sales.

plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: It does not make crypto gains tax-free; you still owe tax on them, the platform just will not report them.

income.justification: A proposed constitutional amendment about the size of the Supreme Court has no income effects to distribute.

plain_json.effective: Only if two-thirds of both chambers pass it and 38 states ratify it
plain_json.plain: It failed in the House on September 2, 2026 (212 to 206, with two-thirds needed), so nothing changes.

timing.justification: Article V process; House vote of 2026-09-02.

rights.justification: It would fix the number of justices at nine, which is a change to the structure of a branch of government rather than to anyone's rights or remedies; the flag vocabulary has no entry for it.

plain_json.one_sentence: Would write into the Constitution that the Supreme Court has exactly nine justices, so no future Congress could add or remove seats.
plain_json.status_plain: Failed a House vote (needed two-thirds; got 212 to 206)
plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: Even if it had passed the House, it would still have needed the Senate and 38 state legislatures.

income.magnitude_note: The Treasury estimated the reporting law's compliance cost at roughly $22 billion in its first year and a few billion a year after that; repeal removes that cost and the anti-money-laundering data with it.
income.justification: The savings go to owners of corporations, LLCs and similar entities, a group that skews toward higher-income households, while the public gives up a tool against money laundering. The reporting duty fell hardest on very small entities, which keeps the score out of the higher bands.

sources.ref: FinCEN regulatory impact analysis of the beneficial ownership rule, 2022

households_business.magnitude_note: About 32 million existing entities were covered by the reporting law before the Treasury exempted domestic companies by rule in March 2025; repeal would make that exemption permanent and extend it to foreign-registered companies.
households_business.justification: Small businesses and single-owner LLCs are the direct beneficiaries: no ownership filings, no penalties for missing them. Households see almost no direct effect. The cost is diffuse: less information for investigators tracing shell companies.

plain_json.plain: Nothing changes until it passes; today the reporting rule is already suspended for U.S. companies by a Treasury regulation, which a future Treasury could reverse.

timing.justification: The bill contains a repeal with no dates.

flags.plain: Repeals the statute behind the Treasury's beneficial-ownership reporting rule, so the rule and its penalties fall with it.

plain_json.one_sentence: Repeals the law that made small companies report who really owns them to the Treasury's anti-money-laundering office.
plain_json.status_plain: Still just a proposal - most bills never get a vote

if_you_are.retiree: No direct effect unless you hold rental property or investments in an LLC.
if_you_are.small_business_owner: You would never have to file an ownership report, and the penalties for missing one would disappear.

plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: It does not touch the separate bank rules that ask who owns a company when it opens an account.

income.magnitude_note: No direct federal spending; the cost is the price of documents (a passport runs about $130 to $165, a birth certificate $15 to $40) and the time to appear in person. An independent survey estimated roughly 9 percent of adult citizens, about 21 million people, do not have citizenship documents readily available.
income.justification: The bill creates no benefit to distribute; it adds a cost to registering, and that cost lands on people who lack a passport or an easily retrievable birth certificate, a group that skews lower-income, older, and includes married women whose current name differs from their birth certificate. A burden concentrated at the bottom scores positive. The effect per person is small, which keeps it out of the higher bands.

sources.ref: Brennan Center / University of Maryland survey on citizenship documents, 2023

households_business.magnitude_note: Applies to every new federal voter registration; no business provisions.
households_business.justification: Households registering or re-registering to vote must produce proof of citizenship in person or through a state-designed alternative; households that never re-register see no change, which is the 0 end of the range. No provision reaches businesses.

plain_json.effective: on enactment, for registrations after that date
plain_json.plain: Would apply to anyone registering or re-registering after it became law; it has passed the House and is waiting in the Senate.

timing.justification: The text sets no dates; states would have to build the checking programs after enactment.

flags.plain: Sets a federal proof-of-citizenship requirement for registration that overrides state registration rules, including mail and online registration without documents.
Lets a private person sue an election official who registers someone without documentary proof of citizenship.
Creates criminal penalties for election officials who register an applicant without the required proof.
Requires states to run ongoing programs to identify and remove non-citizens from voter rolls and to create an alternative documentation process.

rights.justification: Sections 2 and 3 as described in the CRS summary; the election-rules flag is factual, with no prediction of who gains.

plain_json.one_sentence: Requires anyone registering to vote in federal elections to show proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate, and makes states check their voter rolls for non-citizens.
plain_json.status_plain: Passed the House, waiting on the Senate

if_you_are.worker: If you move and register at a new address, you would need to bring proof of citizenship in person.
if_you_are.parent: The same rule would apply when your children register at 18.
if_you_are.retiree: A driver's license alone would not be enough unless it shows citizenship; a passport or birth certificate would.
if_you_are.disability: Mail-in and online registration without documents would end; your state would have to offer an alternative way to prove citizenship.

plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: It does not change what ID you show at the polls on Election Day; it changes how you register.

plain_json.status_plain: Passed the House; its text became law through the Senate bill S. 331

income.magnitude_note: Unpaid leave; no federal spending. Widens who counts as family for existing leave rights and adds up to four hours a year of leave for school and family activities.
income.justification: Job-protected leave matters most to workers who cannot afford to quit or risk dismissal to care for a partner, in-law or adult child, which skews the benefit toward lower- and middle-wage workers. Because the leave is unpaid, higher earners are better placed to use it, which keeps the score from moving further.

households_business.magnitude_note: The Family and Medical Leave Act covers employers with 50 or more employees, so the new obligations fall on larger firms.
households_business.justification: Households gain new job-protected leave to care for domestic partners, parents-in-law, adult children and other relatives, plus short leave for children's school events. Employers already covered by the leave law take on the scheduling and coverage cost; firms under 50 employees are outside it.

sources.ref: Amends the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 and title 5

plain_json.plain: Still in committee; nothing changes unless it passes.

timing.justification: No dates in the title or summary.

rights.justification: Expands an existing statutory right without changing courts, agencies or penalties.

plain_json.one_sentence: Lets workers use family and medical leave to care for a domestic partner, in-law or adult child, and adds a few hours a year to attend a child's school or family events.
plain_json.status_plain: Still just a proposal - most bills never get a vote

if_you_are.worker: If your employer has 50 or more workers, you could take job-protected leave to care for a wider circle of family.
if_you_are.parent: Up to a few hours a year of protected leave for school meetings and activities.
if_you_are.retiree: No direct effect, though an adult child could take leave to care for you.
if_you_are.small_business_owner: No direct effect under 50 employees; larger employers must honor the wider leave.
if_you_are.disability: An adult child or partner with a serious health condition would now be covered by a caregiver's leave.

plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: The leave stays unpaid; this does not create paid family leave.

income.magnitude_note: Moves tip income among restaurant workers; no federal budget effect.
income.justification: Tip pooling with back-of-house staff shifts money from servers to cooks and dishwashers, both low-wage groups, so the score stays near the middle. Employers gain flexibility that can lower what they must pay untipped staff, which nudges the score slightly positive.

households_business.justification: Tipped workers could see their tips shared more widely; untipped coworkers could gain. Restaurant owners gain control over how tips are distributed.

plain_json.plain: In committee; no change unless it passes.

rights.justification: Changes a wage rule, not remedies or enforcement.

plain_json.one_sentence: Lets employers pool tips between servers and kitchen or other staff who don't normally get tips, as long as everyone in the pool is paid at least minimum wage.
plain_json.status_plain: Still just a proposal - most bills never get a vote

if_you_are.worker: If you earn tips, more of them could be shared with coworkers; if you work in the kitchen, you could receive a share.
if_you_are.small_business_owner: You could set up a tip pool that includes back-of-house staff.

plain_json.what_it_does_not_do: It does not let owners or managers keep tips.
